title: Evaluate-and-Repair for LLM-Generated NetOps Changes: A Preregistered Generate–Verify–Repair Study with a Deterministic Net Verifier
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (N=300 canonical device tasks) that evaluated whether a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline—an LLM proposer plus a deterministic network verifier that gates acceptance and supplies counterexamples for automated repair—reduces the acceptance of unsafe or policy‑violating device‑level NetOps proposals in a seeded sandbox. Design (preregistered): within‑task paired comparison on 300 canonical tasks (routing 150 / ACL 100 / BGP 50); proposer = gpt‑5‑mini; arms: LLM‑only (baseline) and guarded GVR (verifier gate + up to one automated repair). Primary estimand: paired absolute reduction in the proportion of proposals that would, if applied, create an unsafe or policy‑violating sandbox state. Results: complete pairs = 300; baseline unsafe proposals = 1/300 (0.3333%); guarded unsafe proposals = 0/300 (0.00%); paired absolute reduction = 0.3333 percentage points; McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) 95% CI for absolute reduction = [0.00, 0.01]. The single baseline unsafe case was corrected by the automated repair under the guarded flow (task‑000165). All prompts, raw responses, provider calls, verifier traces, repair context, and analysis artifacts are archived and hashed for reproducibility (see Disclosure).

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are proposed to convert operator intent into device configurations for NetOps. Their stochastic generation can produce syntactically plausible but operationally unsafe changes (hallucinated routes, permissive ACLs, etc.). Operational adoption therefore depends on reliable architectural safeguards that convert probabilistic proposals into deterministic, auditable decisions. We ask (preregistered): Does a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline—LLM proposer + deterministic network verifier + automated repair—reduce the proportion of proposals that would cause unsafe or policy‑violating sandbox states compared with LLM alone? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001) with deterministic outcome rules and full provenance; (2) an implemented gated verifier + one‑iteration automated repair loop and an exemplar repaired episode (task‑000165) archived with exact hashes; (3) a concise evidence summary showing observed effect sizes and operational implications given the canonical task distribution.
sections.related_work: The GVR idea appears in code and compliance literature as a way to constrain stochastic generation using deterministic oracles (Cadenas, ssrn:6754899). In networking, formal/static verification (Header Space/SEFL/SymNet, and packet‑reachability tooling) provide deterministically checkable properties; prior NetOps/agentic surveys emphasise gated tool scopes, contracts and canary/rollback procedures for safe action (Bilal et al., arXiv:2605.12729). Our study differs by preregistering a confirmatory paired design, freezing verifier decision rules prior to execution, and archiving the entire execution artifact set and hashes for exact replay.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and provenance. The study preregistration id is CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001 (SHA‑256: 156e87e6ce4a9a2348525fa8960f35fb4120031344cf4b4a38b247b10893181b). The preregistration froze task taxonomy, sampling seed, proposer model, verifier checks, repair budget (≤1), primary estimand, analysis plan, missingness rules, and stopping rules. Task bank and sampling. Deterministic stratified sampling (seed 2026‑08‑25) produced 300 canonical device tasks: routing (150), ACL (100), BGP (50). Proposer and orchestration. Proposer model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API). Adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model configuration archived at execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Outcome definition (frozen). Primary binary outcome per task: "would‑cause‑unsafe‑state‑if‑applied". The verifier flags a proposal as unsafe if any of the following verifier checks (deterministic and preregistered) hold when the proposal is hypothetically applied in the sandbox: 1) Reachability analysis: the proposal introduces unintended reachability (new flows becoming reachable that violate the prior reachability specification) as determined by header‑space style reachability comparison; 2) ACL/policy enforcement check: the proposal creates an explicit policy violation (e.g., previously denied traffic becomes allowed against the canonical policy); 3) Syntax/semantic parsing failure: the generated device patch is unparseable or semantically invalid according to the canonical device model; 4) Deterministic safety predicates (preregistered): any non‑reversible change that removes required connectivity or breaks mandatory deny‑by‑default constraints. The verifier implementation and frozen decision rules are archived (execution/transformation_manifest.json; SHA‑256: f3ac546043ac61cb7222b01c975a3cb98d8f309bb7f65f636ab98667e98608b5). GVR repair loop (frozen): guarded flow applies verifier gate; on verifier rejection the verifier returns a structured counterexample; the proposer is re‑invoked once (repair budget = 1) with the counterexample as repair context. Handling missingness/contamination: preregistered deterministic rules exclude tasks requiring vendor‑proprietary features unrepresentable in the canonical model; generation failures are recorded and deterministically handled (none excluded in the completed run). Statistical analysis (frozen): primary test = McNemar exact two‑sided on paired binary outcomes; paired bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) for CI on absolute paired difference. All raw responses, provider calls, and scoring JSONs were archived (see Disclosure and execution_manifest).
sections.results: Execution provenance. Run completed 2026‑08‑25. Planned episodes = 600; completed = 600; hosted model calls used = 301 (300 initial + 1 repair). All raw outputs, provider calls, verifier traces and scoring JSONs archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256: 68c8168fff763b5530f4b36681a8956f5bbfb4ff98f6753a12cae97b017ee8e1). Confirmatory contingency (paired) counts: safe both = 299; unsafe baseline only = 1; unsafe guarded only = 0; unsafe both = 0. Observed rates: baseline unsafe = 1/300 = 0.3333% (Clopper–Pearson 95% CI 0.00844%–1.226%); guarded unsafe = 0/300 = 0.00% (95% CI 0%–0.994%). Paired absolute reduction = 0.3333 percentage points (0.003333 proportion). McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.00 (discordant counts b=1, c=0). Paired bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) 95% CI for absolute reduction = [0.00, 0.01]. Representative repaired episode (artifact pointers). Task ID: task-000165. Artifacts (archived): execution/responses/task-000165-baseline.txt (SHA‑256: 4c4df2ec851732cd7a6302211bbc79b5099a1bf6d470204b6ac883446bcd09f2); execution/responses/task-000165-guarded.txt (SHA‑256: b4faabeaaf3bd9e0fae78adc1bbb3b40ff36d95e95ac6796c2f0000c2af2b8ff); repair provider call: execution/provider_calls/task-000165-guarded-repair.json (SHA‑256: 93d0712d93248452202c8a1f0051ca4a619a1c835a9af1f828494aed1f033ebc); verifier scoring traces: execution/scoring/task-000165-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000165-guarded.json (see execution_manifest). Sequence (archived): baseline generation → verifier rejection with structured counterexample (verifier trace archived) → one automated repair call using that counterexample → repaired proposal passed verifier. All three artifacts cited above are preserved for independent audit and replay. Reproducibility recipe (minimal files to reproduce confirmatory table/figure): execution/raw_results.jsonl (68c8168fff...e8e1), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (7df39740a15b...), execution/model_configuration.json (a40e96e212ab...), execution/transformation_manifest.json (f3ac546043ac...), execution/provider_calls/task-000165-guarded-repair.json (93d0712d93...), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (3421adb52d...). These files plus the archived analysis scripts reproduce reported statistics (see Disclosure for full path and hashes).
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The gated GVR flow corrected the single verifier‑detectable unsafe baseline proposal (task‑000165), demonstrating that a deterministic verifier plus a one‑iteration automated repair loop can remediate verifier‑visible generation errors. However, unsafe proposals were rare in this canonical task distribution (1/300), limiting statistical sensitivity: small absolute reductions correspond to large relative gains but wide uncertainty. Practical implications. Where verifier‑visible failure classes (reachability regressions, explicit ACL policy violations, parse errors) dominate operational risk, gating and automated repair can be integrated into change pipelines to reduce verifier‑detectable hazards. Broader production readiness requires extending verifier coverage (vendor semantics, coupled multi‑change interactions) and scaled evaluations on higher‑risk task strata. Threats to validity. Internal: single proposer (gpt‑5‑mini) and single verifier implementation; Construct: the verifier models canonical device semantics (reachability, ACL/policy checks, parse validity) but intentionally omits certain vendor‑specific coupled behaviors—these limits and verifier traces are archived (execution/transformation_manifest.json; SHA‑256: f3ac5460...). External: canonical tasks differ from heterogeneous production change distributions. Statistical: rare baseline failure reduces power; emphasis is on effect estimates and CIs rather than binary significance. Future work should (i) evaluate targeted high‑risk strata or larger N, (ii) test multiple proposer models, and (iii) extend verifier modeling to vendor features and multi‑change semantics.
sections.conclusion: In a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (N=300), a verifier‑gated GVR pipeline eliminated the single verifier‑detectable unsafe baseline proposal (1→0). Observed absolute reduction = 0.3333 percentage points; p (McNemar exact two‑sided) = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01]. The run validates the mechanics and reproducibility of a deterministic verifier + repair loop for verifier‑visible failure classes and supplies full provenance for independent replay. Given the low baseline prevalence in this canonical sample, larger or stratified studies are needed to quantify modest relative improvements robustly before broad operational claims are made.

After the autonomy lock the AI system autonomously performed literature discovery, research‑gap selection, preregistration, experiment design, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, autonomous peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting. Models and frameworks used (archived): proposer model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API; all provider call logs archived), orchestration adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 (adapter and execution harness archived), deterministic verifier = canonical header‑space/reachability‑style verifier implemented for the sandbox (implementation and verifier traces archived). Exact master prompt and task templates were preserved and hashed. Preregistration: CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001 (SHA‑256: 156e87e6ce4a9a2348525fa8960f35fb4120031344cf4b4a38b247b10893181b). These artifacts plus the archived analysis scripts reproduce the reported statistics and figures.
limitations: Single‑model limitation: experiments used one proposer model (gpt‑5‑mini); results do not establish multi‑model generality.
Synthetic/canonical task set: tasks were deterministic canonical templates (routing/ACL/BGP); production change distributions may have higher base failure rates and different failure modes.

Verifier scope: the deterministic verifier modeled a canonical subset of device semantics and policy checks; some coupled reachability+policy failure modes and vendor‑specific semantics lie outside its coverage (see execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256: f3ac5460...).

Sample size for rare failures: baseline unsafe proposals were rare (1/300), so statistical power to detect moderate relative reductions is limited; larger or higher‑risk datasets are needed to measure modest effects robustly.
Sandbox abstraction: the sandbox simulates canonical device semantics but is not a substitute for vendor‑specific device execution; production deployment requires expanded validation.
